plain: The bankruptcy principle that each layer of creditors must be paid in full before the layer below gets anything, with shareholders last.
desk: Under absolute priority, equity gets zero.

plain: In the US, someone wealthy enough (about $1m of wealth not counting their home, or $200k a year of income) to be allowed into private funds like hedge funds.
desk: We can only take accredited investors in this vehicle.

plain: An investor that buys a big stake in a company and then pushes for changes, such as buybacks, asset sales or new management, to lift the share price.
desk: The activist wants two board seats and a spin-off.

plain: Historical prices rescaled for share splits and dividends, so a chart shows what an investor really experienced rather than fake jumps.
desk: Always backtest on adjusted closes.

plain: Being traded against by someone who knows more than you. The trades you get are the ones you'd rather not have.
desk: Everything we bought this morning went down: classic adverse selection.

plain: Any trading where a computer program sends the orders. It covers both execution algorithms (how to carry out a decided order) and strategies that decide what to trade.
desk: Most of the volume in that pair is algo trading now.

plain: An investor that hands money to fund managers rather than picking investments itself, such as a pension fund, endowment, sovereign wealth fund or family office.
desk: Three allocators are in due diligence with us.

plain: The part of a return that comes from skill rather than from simply being exposed to the market. What investors pay hedge fund fees for.
desk: Strip out the beta and there is no alpha left.

plain: Splitting a fund's return into the part explained by the market and common factors (beta) and the part left over (alpha), usually with a regression, to see how much is genuine skill.
desk: Run the alpha separation before we talk fees.

plain: Unusual data, like satellite images, card spending or web traffic, used to spot trends before official figures come out.
desk: The alt data's pointing to a weak quarter.

plain: A large investor that commits a big first allocation to a new fund, usually in return for lower fees or other special terms.
desk: The anchor took the founders' class at 1 and 15.

plain: The yearly cost of a loan or credit card, including compulsory fees, so different loans can be compared fairly. UK lenders must show it.
desk: The card's 24.9% APR, but the promo rate's zero for a year.

plain: A trader who buys something where it's cheap and sells the same (or nearly the same) thing where it's dear, which pulls the two prices back together.
desk: The arbs will close that gap in seconds.

plain: The mid price at the moment an order reaches the trader or algo. Used as a starting line for measuring how well the order was worked.
desk: We finished 8 bp worse than arrival.

plain: The lowest price anyone is currently willing to sell at. If you buy straight away, this is what you pay. Also called the offer.
desk: Lift the offer, I need them now.

plain: A group of things you can buy that behave in a similar way and make money in a similar way: equities, bonds, FX, commodities, derivatives.
desk: Gold's had a better year than any other asset class.

plain: A firm hired to invest someone else's money for a fee: hedge funds, long-only funds, private equity.
desk: We're one of their three external managers.

plain: Whoever actually owns the money: pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, family offices. They often hire asset managers to invest it.
desk: The big asset owners are cutting hedge fund allocations.

plain: How much money a fund manager looks after for its clients.
desk: They're running about 20 billion of AUM.

plain: A line a curve gets closer and closer to but never touches.
How governments usually sell new bonds: they say how much they want to borrow, investors put in bids, and the best bids win.
desk: The 10-year auction tailed, so yields jumped.

plain: The freeze on debt payments and lawsuits that starts the moment a company files for bankruptcy, stopping creditors grabbing assets.
desk: The stay stops the lenders seizing the planes.

plain: The average price paid for a position built up in several buys, weighted by how many shares each buy was.
desk: Average cost is 81.20, so we're up a couple of quid.

plain: How many shares (or contracts) normally trade in a day. An order's size as a share of ADV tells you how hard it will be to trade.
desk: It's 2% of ADV, we can do it today.

plain: Testing a trading strategy on past data to see how it would have performed. Useful, but easy to fool yourself with.
desk: Great backtest. What about live?

plain: Money that commercial banks hold in their own accounts at the central bank. Banks use reserves to pay each other, and the central bank sets the interest paid on them.
desk: Reserves are still abundant, so the overnight rate sits on the floor.

plain: The number being multiplied over and over. In 2 to the power x, the base is 2.
The international rules, agreed after 2008, that make banks hold more capital and liquid assets so they can survive bad years.
desk: Basel III's made it expensive for banks to hold inventory.

plain: One hundredth of 1%. So 25 basis points is 0.25%.
desk: The Bank hiked 25 bps.

plain: Buying government bonds and selling bond futures against them to capture the small price gap between the two, financed with heavy borrowing through repo.
desk: The Treasury basis trade unwound in March 2020.

plain: A group of shares bought or sold together as one trade, to back a theme or hedge a set of risks.
desk: We hedged the Japan longs with a custom basket.

plain: The index a fund is measured against, like the FTSE 100 or S&P 500.
desk: We beat the benchmark by 2% this year.

plain: A broker's duty to get its client the best overall result: price, cost, speed and the chance of the trade actually happening.
desk: Compliance wants to see the best-ex report.

plain: How much an investment moves with the market. A beta of 0.4 means it tends to move 0.4% for every 1% the market moves.
desk: Our beta-adjusted net is only 15%.

plain: Net exposure after weighting each position by its beta, so jumpy stocks count for more. It shows how much a book really moves with the market.
desk: We are flat in dollars but 20% beta-adjusted long.

plain: The highest price anyone is currently willing to buy at. If you sell straight away, this is what you get.
desk: Hit the bid and get me out.

plain: The gap between the price a market maker will buy at (the bid) and sell at (the ask). It's how market makers earn their money.
desk: The spread's blown out to 3 pips.

plain: The days before a central bank meeting when its officials stop talking publicly about policy. At the Fed it runs from the second Saturday before the meeting to the day after.
desk: Fed's in blackout, so this week it's all about the data.

plain: A loan cut into tradable pieces: the borrower (a government or company) promises fixed interest payments and to repay the face value on a set date. Investors can buy and sell it before then.
desk: We're long 10-year bonds into the data.

plain: When a bond trades above 100 (its face value), because its coupon is higher than the yield the market now wants.
desk: The 2035s are trading at a big premium since yields fell.

plain: Collecting orders from big investors (how many shares or bonds, at what price) to decide the price of a new issue.
desk: The book's covered three times over.

plain: The yearly fee a short seller pays to borrow shares, charged on their value. Tiny for most shares, huge for the most popular shorts.
desk: Borrow's gone from 50 bp to 8% this week.

plain: A payment one side of a merger must make to the other if it walks away or the deal fails for certain reasons, such as a regulator blocking it.
desk: There's a big reverse break fee, so the buyer really wants this closed.

plain: A firm that trades on a client's behalf as its agent, for a commission. The client keeps the market risk; the broker owes it best execution.
desk: Put it through the broker, agency.

plain: The biggest global investment banks that do everything: advice, new issues, trading, research and prime brokerage.
desk: She's at a bulge bracket on the FX desk.

plain: Firms that invest money and are paid according to how their investments do: hedge funds, pension funds, fund managers.
desk: He moved from the sell side to the buy side.

plain: Buying shares back to close a short position, so they can be returned to the lender.
desk: We covered half into the results.

plain: A forced purchase to close a short, usually because the lender recalled the shares and no one else would lend them.
desk: They recalled 200k and we're getting bought in.

plain: Lots of people trying to buy at once, pushing the price up. The opposite is selling pressure.
desk: Real buying pressure in gold today.

plain: Compound annual growth rate: the steady yearly rate that takes you from a start value to an end value.
desk: The fund's done 11% CAGR over five years.

plain: The right, but not the obligation, to buy something at a set price (the strike) before a set date. The most you can lose is the price you paid for it (the premium).
desk: Buy calls: you keep the upside and know your worst case.

plain: The amount of money a strategy can run before trading costs eat its profits. Bigger funds move prices more, so every strategy has a limit.
desk: Great Sharpe, but there's no capacity in small caps.

plain: A prime broker introducing hedge funds to investors such as pension funds and family offices. Free, but the PB expects trading business in return.
desk: Cap intro got us in front of three endowments.

plain: Trading one of a company's securities against another (its loans, bonds, CDS or shares) when their prices tell inconsistent stories about the same business.
desk: Classic cap structure arb: buy CDS protection, short the equity.

plain: The moment holders give up and sell at any price, often near the bottom of a fall.
desk: Volume's huge, that looks like capitulation.

plain: The share of a private equity or property fund's profits that goes to the manager, usually 20%, paid only after investors get their money back plus a preferred return.
desk: The partners' carried interest only kicks in above an 8% pref.

plain: Borrowing in a currency with low interest rates to hold one with higher rates, earning the gap. It pays steadily, then loses fast if the low-rate currency suddenly jumps.
desk: The yen carry trade unwound in a week.

plain: The share of a bank's customer deposits it must leave frozen at the central bank. The higher it is, the less the bank can lend. The CBN's is about 45%; the Fed's has been zero since 2020.
desk: CBN kept the CRR at 45%, so naira liquidity stays tight.

plain: The event that will make the market see what you see and move the price, like results day or a central bank meeting.
desk: What's the catalyst, and when?

plain: The bank behind a country's banks: it sets the main interest rate, issues the currency, holds banks' reserves and lends to them in a panic. Examples: the Fed, the ECB, the Bank of England, the CBN.
desk: Everything this week is about what the central banks say.

plain: The list of what a central bank owns (mainly bonds bought through QE) and what it owes (mainly banks' reserves and banknotes). QE makes both sides bigger; QT makes them smaller.
desk: The Fed's balance sheet is still about $6.7 trillion.

plain: Letting the central bank set interest rates without politicians telling it what to do, so it can make unpopular decisions to keep inflation low. Politicians set the goal; the bank chooses how to reach it.
desk: Any hint of pressure on the Fed's independence and the long end sells off.

plain: The official record of who owns which securities, kept electronically: DTC in the US, CREST in the UK, CSCS in Nigeria.
desk: It's sitting in CREST, no paper certificates.

plain: The part of US bankruptcy law that lets a company keep operating while it reorganises its debts under a court's protection.
desk: They filed Chapter 11 last night.

plain: One of the many small orders a big order is cut into before being sent to the market.
desk: The algo is sending child orders of a few hundred shares.

plain: An automatic pause in trading when a market falls too far, too fast, to give everyone time to think.
desk: We hit the 7% circuit breaker, trading's halted.

plain: A rule making a manager pay back performance fees already taken if later losses wipe out the gains. Rare in hedge funds, common in private equity.
desk: The LPA has a clawback, but good luck enforcing it.

plain: A bond's quoted price, leaving out the interest earned since the last coupon. The buyer pays the clean price plus that accrued interest (the dirty price).
desk: Screens show clean; settlement's on dirty.

plain: Everything between agreeing a trade and settling it: confirming the details, working out who owes what, and managing the risk in between.
desk: It's cleared, so the CCP is our counterparty now.

plain: A firm that steps in between buyer and seller and guarantees both sides, so neither loses out if the other goes bust.
desk: It's cleared, so we're not worried about the other side.

plain: A specialist bank that settles most large FX trades by releasing both currencies only once both have arrived, removing settlement risk.
desk: Push it through CLS, no Herstatt risk.

plain: When two prices each wander unpredictably but a particular combination of them, the spread, keeps returning to an average, like a dog on a lead.
desk: Test whether the pair is still cointegrated.

plain: A fund that buys hundreds of leveraged loans and pays investors in slices: the top slices are paid first and safest, the bottom slice takes the first losses.
desk: CLO demand is propping up loan prices.

plain: In the US, the legal name for a manager who trades futures for clients. Trend-following hedge funds are called CTAs because most of them trade futures.
desk: The CTAs are all long gold now that the trend has turned.

plain: The team that makes sure a firm and its staff follow the law and the firm's own rules. The first call whenever you're unsure.
desk: Run it past compliance before you take the call.

plain: Earning returns on your returns, so each period's gain becomes part of what grows next.
desk: Over 30 years, compounding does most of the work.

plain: The average forecast from analysts: what the market expects. Results are judged against it.
desk: Profits came in 5% above consensus.

plain: One feed that combines the quotes and trades from every venue into a single official record.
desk: The print showed up on the tape a moment later.

plain: Trouble in one firm or market spreading to others, often through shared positions or forced selling.
desk: The worry is contagion into the other banks.

plain: The share price at which converting a convertible bond into shares breaks even: the bond's face value divided by the number of shares it converts into.
desk: Stock's at 45, conversion price is 50.

plain: Buying a company's convertible bond and shorting its shares to cancel most of the share-price risk, earning from the coupon, rehedging as the shares move, and any mispricing in the bond's built-in option.
desk: Convert arb funds were levered 8 to 10 times going into 2008.

plain: A bond that the holder can swap for a fixed number of the company's shares. It pays a lower coupon than a plain bond because of that built-in option.
desk: New converts from tech issuers this week.

plain: The bend in a bond's price-yield curve: prices rise more when yields fall than they drop when yields rise by the same amount.
desk: Long bonds give you convexity, so you're paid for big moves.

plain: Anything a company does that changes its securities: dividends, splits, rights issues, spin-offs, mergers, buybacks.
desk: Check the corporate actions calendar before you cover.

plain: How much two things move together, from +1 (always together) through 0 (unrelated) to -1 (always opposite). Low correlation is what makes spreading money around reduce risk.
desk: Correlations went to one in the sell-off.

plain: The risk that whoever is on the other side of a deal (a bank, a broker, a borrower) fails and doesn't pay or deliver what it owes.
desk: Spread it across two PBs, the counterparty risk is too big.

plain: The interest a bond pays each year, usually as a percentage of what you lent. A 5% coupon on 100 pounds pays 5 pounds a year.
desk: It's a 10-year with a 4% coupon.

plain: Insurance-like contract on a borrower: the buyer pays a yearly premium and is paid out if the borrower defaults. Also used to bet that a borrower will get into trouble.
desk: We bought five-year CDS on the bank as a hedge.

plain: A grade from an agency such as S&P, Moody's or Fitch saying how likely a borrower is to repay. BBB- and above is investment grade; below that is high yield.
desk: A downgrade to BB makes it a fallen angel.

plain: The extra interest a borrower pays above a risk-free rate (such as a government bond) because there's a chance it won't pay back.
desk: Credit spreads widened 40 bps on the growth scare.

plain: When many funds hold the same positions, so if some are forced to sell, prices move against all of them at once.
desk: That short is crowded with the pods; size it small.

plain: The date a performance fee is locked in and paid, usually once a year on 31 December. Before then it is only an estimate that can shrink if the fund falls.
desk: Fees crystallise at year-end, so December matters.

plain: A central bank holding its currency at a fixed rate against another, such as the dollar, by buying and selling it. A peg the economy can't support usually breaks suddenly.
desk: Puts on the peg are nicely asymmetric.

plain: A bond's annual coupon divided by its price: the cash income for what you paid. It ignores any gain or loss as the price moves to 100 at maturity.
desk: Current yield's 5.8 but YTM's 7 because of the pull to par.

plain: Keeping a client's cash, shares and other assets safe in accounts separate from the bank's own.
desk: Assets in custody should be safe if the bank fails.

plain: A trading venue that hides orders until after they've traded, so big orders don't move the price.
desk: We got half the order done in the dark.

plain: Short interest divided by average daily volume: how many days of normal trading it would take for every short to buy back.
desk: Eight days to cover. That's a crowded short.

plain: The gap between a takeover target's share price and the offer price. It is the market's price for the risk that the deal fails, plus the cost of waiting.
desk: The deal spread blew out on the antitrust headline.

plain: A currency hedge that only takes effect if a takeover actually closes, so a buyer paying in a foreign currency is protected without being stuck with the hedge if the deal fails.
desk: The bank priced a deal-contingent hedge for the euro leg.

plain: A firm that quotes prices and trades with clients using its own money, taking the other side of the deal.
desk: Three dealers came back on the RFQ.

plain: A growth factor below 1, so each period keeps only part of what was there.
When a borrower fails to pay interest or repay a loan on time, or breaks the loan's terms. For a company it often leads to a restructuring or bankruptcy.
desk: They missed the coupon; it's a default.

plain: A pot every clearing house member pays into, used to cover a failed member's losses once its own margin runs out.
desk: Our default fund contribution went up again.

plain: Part of a bonus paid over the next few years and lost if you leave early. Often called golden handcuffs.
desk: Half my bonus is deferred over three years.

plain: Prices falling across the economy, the opposite of inflation. It sounds good but is dangerous: people delay buying, and debts get heavier in real terms. Japan struggled with it for years.
desk: The BoJ spent two decades trying to escape deflation.

plain: Cutting positions to reduce borrowing, often by many funds at once, which pushes prices further in the same direction.
desk: This isn't news, it's everyone degrossing at once.

plain: Settling a trade so the securities move only at the same moment as the cash, so neither side can hand over its half and get nothing.
desk: It's DVP, so there's no free delivery.

plain: How much an option or convertible's price moves for each £1 (or $1) move in the underlying share or asset. It tells you how many shares to short to hedge.
desk: Delta's 0.6: short 60 shares per 100 of exposure.

plain: Trading in instruments that move one-for-one with the underlying shares, such as swaps, futures and baskets. Bank delta-one desks build custom hedge baskets for funds.
desk: Ask delta-one to build a basket for the residual.

plain: How much people want to buy at each price. Drawn as the buyers line, which slopes down.
desk: Demand for dollars is strong this morning.

plain: How much a matrix scales area. 2 means areas double; 0 means everything gets squashed flat onto a line.
Your share of a company shrinking because it issued new shares that you didn't buy.
desk: Don't take up the rights and you're diluted.

plain: New loans made to a company during bankruptcy to keep it running. They are repaid ahead of almost all older debt.
desk: The DIP lenders are the safest people in the room.

plain: Market data bought straight from one exchange, arriving faster than the consolidated tape.
desk: The HFTs are all on the direct feeds.

plain: A strategy that makes or loses money mainly from which way prices move, rather than from the gap between related positions.
desk: It is a directional fund dressed up as relative value.

plain: A bond trading below 100 (its face value), because its coupon is lower than the yield the market now wants. Its price rises towards 100 as it nears maturity.
desk: Low-coupon discount bonds are the most rate-sensitive.

plain: The growth you give up by waiting. Used to shrink future money back to what it's worth today.
desk: We're discounting at 6%.

plain: Working backwards from money you'll receive in the future to what it's worth today, by dividing by the interest it could have earned. The opposite of compounding.
desk: Higher rates mean heavier discounting, so long-duration assets sell off.

plain: Trading where a person makes the decisions, using research and judgement, rather than following fixed computer rules.
desk: He's a discretionary macro PM: a few big views, held with conviction.

plain: A vote against the committee's decision by one of its members. Dissents show which way a committee might move next.
desk: Two hawkish dissents tell you they're not done hiking.

plain: Part of a company's profit paid out to the people who own its shares.
desk: They've raised the dividend again.

plain: A chart the Fed publishes four times a year with one dot per official showing where each thinks the policy rate should be at the end of the next few years. Headlines quote the middle (median) dot.
desk: The dots moved up 50 for next year: that's the story, not the hike.

plain: Leaning towards lower interest rates because jobs and growth worry you more than inflation. A dove is a policymaker who thinks this way.
desk: The statement read dovish, so the currency dropped.

plain: How far a portfolio has fallen from its highest point.
desk: He's in a 6% drawdown, so risk is cutting his gross.

plain: The US Fed's two goals, set by Congress: maximum employment and stable prices (2% inflation), with equal weight.
desk: With inflation above target and jobs fine, the dual mandate points one way: hike.

plain: The long standard form an investor sends a fund before investing, covering its strategy, team, risk, operations and legal terms.
desk: IR is buried in DDQs this month.

plain: How sensitive a bond's price is to a change in its yield, measured in years: roughly, the percentage price change for a one-point move in yield. Longer bonds and lower coupons mean higher duration.
desk: We cut duration before the CPI print.

plain: A reason you'll be right when the market is wrong: better information, better interpretation, or more speed.
desk: What's your edge on this trade?

plain: What a rate really pays or costs over a year once compounding is included. UK savings accounts must show it as the AER.
desk: Six-month coupons at 8% are 8.16% effective.

plain: What you actually paid compared with the mid price, doubled so it compares with the quoted spread. Smaller if your price was improved, bigger if your order walked the book.
desk: Quoted was 2 bp but the effective spread was 5 on that size.

plain: The idea that prices already reflect available information, so beating the market consistently is hard. Comes in weak, semi-strong and strong versions.
desk: In a market this efficient, any edge has to come from somewhere others aren't looking.

plain: A newer or smaller fund manager, usually with a short track record. Some investors run programmes that set money aside for them.
desk: The pension has an emerging manager programme with $500m to place.

plain: A hedge fund strategy that trades around company events such as takeovers, spin-offs, restructurings and activist campaigns.
desk: The event-driven book is full of merger spreads right now.

plain: The first day a share trades without its next dividend: buy on or after it and you don't get that dividend. The price usually drops by about the dividend.
desk: It goes ex tomorrow, so it'll open down 50p.

plain: A central, regulated marketplace where standardised things trade under the same public rules for everyone.
desk: It's listed on the exchange, so the price is right there on the screen.

plain: How much a change in the exchange rate shows up in a country's prices. It's high where much is imported or priced in dollars, as in Nigeria.
desk: Pass-through from the naira to food prices is close to one for one.

plain: In a stock-for-stock merger, the number of the buyer's shares paid for each share of the target.
desk: Ratio is 0.8: short 800 buyer shares per 1,000 target.

plain: The average result of a bet if you could make it many times: each outcome times its chance, added up.
desk: Small, but positive EV. Do it ten thousand times.

plain: Shrinking where each step multiplies by the same number below 1. It gets close to zero but never reaches it.
Growth where each step multiplies by the same number, so it grows faster the bigger it gets.
An average where older data gets exponentially smaller weights, so recent days count most.
desk: We use an EWMA vol with lambda 0.94.

plain: How much you gain or lose when something moves. For a single share, the value of the position.
desk: What's our exposure to oil if it drops 10%?

plain: A broad driver that moves many stocks together, such as the whole market, a sector, or a style like cheapness, momentum or company size.
desk: Strip out the factor exposure and there is no alpha left.

plain: A private company that manages the wealth of one very rich family (or a few), often investing directly in funds and deals.
desk: A Gulf family office came in at launch.

plain: Extreme moves happening far more often than a normal distribution predicts.
desk: Markets have fat tails, size for the crash, not the average day.

plain: Exchange-traded contracts that pay out based on the average fed funds rate in a month. Their prices show what the market expects the Fed to do, and are used to work out the odds of a move.
desk: Fed funds futures have about 75% of a December hike priced.

plain: The Fed's policy rate: the overnight rate at which US banks lend reserves to each other. The Fed sets a target range a quarter of a point wide, such as 3.75 to 4.00%.
desk: Fed funds futures price about a 60% chance of a December hike.

plain: Each firm in the chain between a saver and the market taking its own fee, so the costs stack up.
desk: After fee layering, the pension kept barely half the gain.

plain: Fixed income, currencies and commodities: the part of a bank's trading floor that isn't equities.
desk: FICC revenues were up on the quarter.

plain: Fill the whole order right now, or cancel all of it. No partial fills.
desk: It's fill-or-kill, all or nothing.

plain: The margin a lender charges above a benchmark rate such as SOFR. A large fund might borrow at SOFR plus 35 bp, a small one at plus 75.
desk: We got the financing spread down to 40.

plain: Forced selling at whatever price is available, usually because of margin calls or redemptions.
desk: Someone's having a fire sale in credit.

plain: Trading small price gaps between closely related bonds, futures, swaps and yield curves, usually with heavy borrowing because the gaps are measured in basis points.
desk: FI arb is pennies, so it lives or dies on funding.

plain: Orders in the book that are cancelled the moment someone tries to trade against them, so the depth you saw isn't really there.
desk: The bid looked deep, then it all got pulled.

plain: Federal Open Market Committee: the Fed's rate-setting group of 12 voters (the seven governors, the New York Fed president and four other regional presidents in rotation). It meets eight times a year.
desk: FOMC is Wednesday, so nobody wants to add risk before then.

plain: The written account of a central bank meeting, published later (three weeks later for the Fed), showing how many members leaned which way and what worried them.
desk: The minutes said 'most participants' saw another hike as appropriate.

plain: A lender selling your positions for you because you didn't meet a margin call, at whatever the market will pay.
desk: He got liquidated at the lows.

plain: A quarterly US filing listing a fund manager's long holdings in US shares, required above $100 million. Shorts aren't shown.
desk: Their 13F shows they doubled the position.

plain: A central bank telling markets what it expects to do with rates in future. Because markets act on it straight away, the words themselves move longer-term interest rates.
desk: The forward guidance was the real decision; the hold was priced in.

plain: The same thing trading on many venues at once, so its buyers and sellers are spread across lots of order books.
desk: Liquidity's so fragmented you need a router just to find it.

plain: Trading ahead of a client's large order because you know it's coming. Illegal.
desk: That's front-running, surveillance will catch it.

plain: The layer of a company's debt where its value runs out: layers above are paid in full, layers below get little or nothing. It usually becomes the new owners' shares.
desk: The unsecureds are the fulcrum.

plain: An independent firm that works out what a fund is worth and keeps its investor records, so investors don't rely on the manager's word.
desk: The administrator signs off the monthly NAV.

plain: A fund that invests in other hedge funds, spreading money across many managers and doing the research and checks for its investors.
desk: A fund of funds redeemed from us after one bad quarter.

plain: How fast delta changes as the price moves. A hedged position with positive gamma makes money from moves in either direction.
desk: Long gamma: we like it when the stock moves.

plain: Paid time off a departing employee must take before joining a rival, so they cannot take fresh information or clients with them.
desk: He is on twelve months of garden leave before he can start.

plain: A fund rule that caps how much money can be taken out in one period, for example 25% of the fund a quarter. Anything over the cap waits.
desk: Redemptions were 40% of the fund, so the gate kicked in.

plain: Shares that are easy and cheap to borrow, with a fee well under 1% a year. Most big shares, most of the time.
desk: It's GC, borrow's not an issue.

plain: The firm that runs a fund set up as a partnership: it makes the investment decisions and earns the fees. The investors are the limited partners (LPs).
desk: The GP put in 10% of the fund from the founders' own money.

plain: A bond issued by the UK government, sold at auctions run by the Debt Management Office.
desk: Gilts sold off after the budget.

plain: In FX, a trade done with one bank and then handed over to the client's prime broker, which becomes the bank's counterparty.
desk: Trade with whoever's best, it all gets given up.

plain: A hedge fund style that bets on whole economies, through currencies, interest rates, bonds, commodities and stock indices.
desk: The macro funds are all short the yen into the meeting.

plain: An order that stays live until it fills or you cancel it, often for up to about 90 days.
desk: Leave it GTC at that level.

plain: Longs plus shorts as a percentage of the fund's own money. Above 100% means it's using borrowed money.
desk: We're running 180% gross.

plain: What you multiply by each period. 5% growth is a growth factor of 1.05.
How much less than a security's value a lender will lend against it. A 2% haircut means you can borrow 98.
desk: They've raised the haircut on that bond to 10.

plain: A share that few people will lend because so many want to short it, so the borrow fee is high (over 10% a year) and recalls are likely.
desk: It's gone HTB, we're paying 25%.

plain: Leaning towards higher interest rates because inflation worries you more than jobs and growth. A hawk is a policymaker who thinks this way.
desk: A hawkish hold: no move, but they signalled more hikes.

plain: A fund that tries to make money whichever way markets go. It can bet on falls, borrow to invest more, and charges a share of profits.
desk: The fund's net short going into earnings.

plain: Someone who trades to reduce a risk they already have, like an exporter locking in an exchange rate, rather than to make a trading profit.
desk: That's hedger flow, they'll sell whatever the price.

plain: An order worked by hand by a human trader, rather than handed to an algorithm (low touch). Used for difficult, illiquid or sensitive orders.
desk: It's a thin name, keep it high touch.

plain: Bonds and loans from riskier borrowers, rated below investment grade, which pay higher interest to make up for the extra risk.
desk: HY spreads are 50 wider on the week.

plain: Quant trading where speed is the edge: computers react in microseconds and hold positions for seconds or less, often as market makers.
desk: The HFTs pulled their quotes the second the number came out.

plain: The previous peak. After losses, a manager must get back above it before earning performance pay again.
desk: She's below her high-water mark, so no payout yet.

plain: A return a fund must beat before it can charge a performance fee, often the cash rate or a fixed 4 to 8%. Hard hurdles charge only on the excess; soft ones charge on everything once beaten.
desk: The hurdle is SOFR, so cash has to be beaten first.

plain: An order that shows only a small slice of its size and refills as each slice trades, hiding how big it really is.
desk: There's an iceberg sitting on the bid.

plain: The part of a stock's move that belongs to the company alone (its products, management, earnings surprises), after market, sector, country and factor moves are taken out.
desk: 80% of our risk is idiosyncratic, which is what we want.

plain: Fill whatever can be filled right now and cancel the rest, so nothing is left showing.
desk: Send it IOC.

plain: The full cost of an order compared with the price when the decision to trade was made. Also the name of an algo that trades fast early to keep that cost down.
desk: We matched VWAP but the IS was 40 bp.

plain: The amount of future price movement that an option's price assumes. If the asset actually moves more, the option was cheap.
desk: Implied vol on the convert is 30; the stock's realising 40.

plain: The rate at which prices rise, so each pound (or naira) buys a bit less each year.
desk: UK inflation came in at 3%.

plain: What people and markets expect inflation to be in future. They matter because they feed into pay claims and price setting, so they can make inflation self-fulfilling.
desk: Five-year breakevens are drifting up; expectations are the Fed's worry.

plain: The inflation rate a central bank promises to aim for, almost always 2% a year for the big central banks.
desk: Inflation's been above target for five years now.

plain: Other traders working out that you have a big order from the pattern of your trades, and trading ahead of you.
desk: The algo was too regular, we had leakage all afternoon.

plain: Orders from traders who know, or have worked out, where the price is going next. Market makers lose money trading against it.
desk: That client's flow is toxic, widen them out.

plain: The deposit needed to open a leveraged position, as a percentage of its value.
desk: Initial's 50%, so you can buy twice your cash.

plain: A company's first sale of shares to the public, when it lists on a stock exchange and the company gets the money.
desk: The IPO popped 30% on day one.

plain: Trading on material non-public information. A crime in the UK and the US.
desk: He was done for insider dealing on a takeover.

plain: The price of borrowing money: the rent a borrower pays a lender, as a percentage of the amount per year.
desk: Every price on the screen is built on interest rates.

plain: The band set by a central bank's two overnight windows: the rate at which banks can borrow from it (the ceiling) and the rate it pays on money left with it (the floor). Overnight market rates trade inside it.
desk: The CBN moved the corridor to +50/-300 around the MPR.

plain: A contract where two sides swap interest payments, usually fixed for floating. Funds use swaps to bet on where interest rates will go without buying bonds.
desk: Receive fixed in two-year swaps if you think the Bank will cut.

plain: The risk a market maker carries from holding a position it took on from a client, which could lose value before it can be passed on.
desk: We're long a lot of it, skew the quotes lower.

plain: Whoever creates and first sells a share or bond: a company or a government. It gets the money from the first sale.
desk: The issuer's coming back for more next month.

plain: A formula for the bet size that grows money fastest, given your odds. Traders usually bet only a fraction of it.
desk: We size at quarter Kelly.

plain: A term that lets investors take their money out early if a named person, usually the founder, leaves or stops running the fund.
desk: The key-person clause triggers if the CIO steps back.

plain: A button or automatic limit that stops all of a firm's trading at once.
desk: Hit the kill switch, the algo's gone wild.

plain: The delay between something happening in the market and you seeing it, or reacting to it.
desk: We cut our latency to under ten microseconds.

plain: The rule that the average of many independent tries gets closer and closer to the expected value. It is why a small edge becomes reliable when repeated many times.
desk: We are not betting on one trade; we are betting on the law of large numbers.

plain: The fee for borrowing physical gold or silver, quoted per year. Normally under 1%, but it jumps when metal runs short.
desk: Silver lease rates are through 30%, someone's getting squeezed.

plain: A central bank lending or buying when nobody else will, to stop a panic.
desk: The Fed's back as lender of last resort.

plain: Controlling more than your own money by borrowing, measured as gross exposure divided by your own money (equity). It makes every move bigger.
desk: We're running three times levered.

plain: A bank loan to a company that already has a lot of debt, usually senior and secured, with interest that rises and falls with short-term rates.
desk: Most leveraged loans end up in CLOs.

plain: The London Interbank Offered Rate: a benchmark built from banks' estimates of what they'd pay to borrow. After rigging scandals it was replaced by rates based on real trades, such as SONIA and SOFR. Dollar LIBOR ended in 2023.
desk: Legacy LIBOR loans had to be moved onto SOFR.

plain: Buy at your price or lower, or sell at your price or higher. The price is certain; being filled isn't.
desk: Leave a bid at 50.

plain: The list of all buy and sell limit orders waiting at each price, with how much is at each. The best bid and ask sit at the top.
desk: Pull up the book before you send that.

plain: US price bands that briefly pause trading in a single stock that moves too far too quickly.
desk: It's in a LULD halt, wait five minutes.

plain: An investor who puts money into a fund but doesn't run it. The fund manager is the general partner (GP).
desk: The LPs want lower fees.

plain: How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price much. Lots of buyers and sellers means liquid; few means illiquid.
desk: Liquidity's thin going into the holidays.

plain: A trading venue that shows orders to everyone before they trade.
desk: Small orders go lit, the block goes dark.

plain: Buying a struggling company's debt, usually the fulcrum, in order to end up owning the company after its restructuring.
desk: They're playing loan-to-own on this one.

plain: Confirmation from a broker that shares are available to borrow, needed before a short sale in most markets.
desk: Can't get a locate, the PB has nothing.

plain: How long new money must stay in a fund before it can be taken out, often 1 to 3 years.
desk: There's a one-year soft lock with a 3% early exit fee.

plain: A fund that only buys (never bets on falls) and is judged against a benchmark like the S&P 500.
desk: Long-only money has been selling tech.

plain: A hedge fund strategy that buys shares it thinks are too cheap and short sells shares it thinks are too expensive. The largest strategy family.
desk: She runs a TMT L/S book at a pod shop.

plain: A term in a merger agreement letting the buyer walk away if something seriously damages the target's business before the deal closes.
desk: Is the buyer trying to call a MAC?

plain: The minimum equity, as a percentage of the position, needed to keep a leveraged position open. Fall below it and you get a margin call.
desk: Maintenance is 25, we've got room.

plain: The side of a trade whose order was already waiting in the book. Makers provide the price and earn the spread.
desk: We're makers on most of our flow, so we collect the rebate.

plain: A fee model that pays a small rebate to orders that wait in the book and charges a fee to orders that trade straight away.
desk: Post passively and collect the rebate.

plain: The yearly fee a fund charges on the money it manages, whatever its returns, usually 1 to 2%. It pays for staff, systems and offices.
desk: The management fee barely covers the team at this size.

plain: The payment a short seller makes to the lender of the shares to replace a dividend the lender would have received.
desk: We owe a manufactured div on the short.

plain: The part of a leveraged account that's really yours: the cushion between the value of your positions and what you owe the lender.
desk: Margin's getting thin on that book.

plain: A lender's demand for more cash or securities because your equity has fallen below the maintenance margin. Not paying means the lender sells.
desk: We got a margin call from the PB this morning.

plain: Revaluing every position at today's market price, every day, whether or not anything has been sold.
desk: Mark the book to the close.

plain: Anywhere buyers and sellers meet and agree a price. It can be a car boot sale, a website or a network of banks.
desk: FX is a 24-hour market with no building.

plain: Insider dealing and market manipulation: anything that cheats other traders or distorts prices.
desk: It's a market abuse risk, don't touch it.

plain: What a whole company is worth at today's share price: the price times the number of shares.
desk: It's a 50 million market cap, so it's small.

plain: The stream of quotes and trades a market produces, plus its history.
desk: Our market data bill went up again.

plain: How much is waiting to be bought and sold at each price beyond the best ones. Shown by Level 2 data.
desk: There's no depth: one big order and it'll gap.

plain: How far your own buying or selling moves the price against you. Part of it fades after you stop; part of it stays.
desk: Thirty percent of ADV? The impact will kill it.

plain: A firm that always quotes a price to buy and a price to sell, earning the gap and trying not to hold a big position either way.
desk: The market makers pulled their quotes in the sell-off.

plain: Buy or sell now at the best price available. Being filled is certain; the price isn't.
desk: Just pay the offer.

plain: The price where the amount people want to buy equals the amount people want to sell. Also called the equilibrium price.
desk: Where's the market in gold right now?

plain: A strategy built so the market's direction barely affects it, usually with net exposure close to zero. It still has risks, especially when it uses a lot of borrowing.
desk: We run market-neutral: net stays within plus or minus 5%.

plain: An order to trade at the official closing auction price. Index funds use them to match their benchmark.
desk: Big MOC imbalance on the buy side tonight.

plain: A limit order priced so it can trade straight away. It fills now like a market order but can't go past its limit.
desk: Send it as a marketable limit so we don't chase it.

plain: A fund set-up where onshore and offshore feeder funds collect investors' money and pass it all into one master fund that does the trading.
desk: It's a standard master-feeder: Delaware and Cayman into a Cayman master.

plain: The exchange's computer that takes orders one at a time and matches them against the book by price and time.
desk: Our servers sit next to the matching engine.

plain: Important facts that aren't public yet. Trading on them is insider dealing, a crime.
desk: You're wall-crossed, so you can't trade it.

plain: A grid of numbers that acts like a machine: feed it an arrow and it hands you back a new one.
desk: Multiply through by the sensitivity matrix.

plain: The tendency of a price or spread that has moved unusually far from its average to drift back towards it.
desk: It's a mean-reversion trade: fade the move.

plain: Buying a company that's being taken over to earn the gap between its share price and the offer price, which pays for the risk that the deal fails.
desk: The arb spread blew out on the antitrust news.

plain: Halfway between the best bid and the best ask. Used as the reference price, but nobody has to trade with you there.
desk: Where's mid? Show me the mid on the screen.

plain: The tendency of assets that have risen recently to keep rising for a while, and of recent losers to keep falling. It can reverse violently.
desk: Momentum crashed when the market bounced.

plain: A central bank creating money to pay for government spending directly. It's banned in the euro area and avoided by independent central banks because it tends to cause high inflation.
desk: Ways and means was monetary financing in all but name.

plain: What a central bank does with interest rates and money to keep inflation near target and the economy steady. Raising rates is tightening; cutting is easing.
desk: Monetary policy works with long lags, so they act on forecasts.

plain: The group that sets interest rates at the Bank of England (9 members) and at the Central Bank of Nigeria (12 members).
desk: The MPC split 8-1, with one vote for 50 bps.

plain: Using two or more prime brokers so one failing, or pulling its financing, can't freeze the whole fund.
desk: Since Lehman, everyone's multi-prime.

plain: A firm that hands money to many independent PM teams (pods), each with its own strict risk limits.
desk: She left the single-manager for a pod shop.

plain: An ordinary fund open to anyone, with strict rules on borrowing, shorting and concentration, and money you can take out any day.
desk: Long-only mutual funds own most of this stock.

plain: Selling shares short without having borrowed them or arranged to. Banned or tightly restricted almost everywhere.
desk: That's not a locate, that's a naked short.

plain: The best price to sell at and the best price to buy at across all US exchanges at that moment.
desk: We filled inside the NBBO.

plain: What a fund is worth: its assets minus what it owes. Per unit, it is the price investors buy in and sell out at.
desk: The admin struck the NAV at 104.2.

plain: Longs minus shorts as a percentage of the fund's own money: how much of a market move the fund catches.
desk: We're 40% net long into the data.

plain: Adding up all the trades between parties and settling only the difference, so far less cash and fewer securities have to move.
desk: After netting we only owe 3,000 shares.

plain: On a platform, the cost of paying winning PMs their share of profits while losing PMs pay nothing back, so payouts can exceed the fund's overall profit.
desk: Netting risk ate most of the gross this year.

plain: The interest rate (after inflation) that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy. It can't be measured directly, only estimated, and estimates differ widely. Written r*.
desk: If r-star is higher than we thought, policy isn't that tight.

plain: The fashionable US growth shares of the late 1960s and early 1970s, such as Xerox, Polaroid and IBM, bought at very high prices on the belief their growth would never slow. They crashed in 1973 and 1974.
desk: This rally feels like the Nifty Fifty all over again.

plain: Nigerian Overnight Financing Rate: the naira overnight benchmark the CBN introduced in April 2026 to replace NIBOR, calculated from actual overnight repo trades between banks.
desk: The new facility is priced at NOFR plus 300.

plain: A trading firm, not a bank, that streams buy and sell prices for others to trade on, using its own capital. Examples are XTX Markets, Citadel Securities and Jump.
desk: The non-bank liquidity providers now make most of the prices in spot EUR/USD.

plain: An FX forward where the currencies never change hands; only the difference is paid, usually in dollars. Used for currencies with capital controls, like the naira.
desk: Foreign funds hedge the naira with NDFs.

plain: A clearing house replacing the original link between buyer and seller with two new ones, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer.
desk: Once it's novated, we face the CCP, not them.

plain: Open, high, low, close and volume for each period: the data behind a candlestick chart.
desk: Just pull daily OHLCV for the last ten years.

plain: The most recently issued government bond of a given maturity, which trades most and costs slightly more. Older bonds of similar maturity are off-the-run.
desk: Long the old tens, short on-the-runs.

plain: When costs stay mostly fixed as a business grows, so each extra pound of revenue is mostly profit. A fund managing five times more money earns five times the fee with roughly the same costs.
desk: Past breakeven, the operating leverage in this business is huge.

plain: The checks an investor runs on a fund's operations before investing: who holds, values and audits the assets, the controls, systems and compliance.
desk: We passed investment due diligence but ODD flagged the administrator.

plain: Returns from skill that have roughly zero correlation with the market, sectors, countries, currencies and factors: what is left after hedging all of those away.
desk: Allocators pay for orthogonal alpha, not beta.

plain: How far the economy's actual output is above (positive) or below (negative) what it could produce without pushing up inflation, as a percentage.
desk: With a positive output gap and sticky services inflation, they can't cut.

plain: Trading done directly between two parties, usually a client and a dealer, with no central order book.
desk: Most of the bond market is OTC.

plain: Building a model that fits past data so closely it has learned the noise rather than the signal, so it disappoints when used for real.
desk: Twelve parameters on five years of data? That's overfitting.

plain: Buying one security and short selling a closely related one, so the shared risk cancels and only the bet that one beats the other is left.
desk: We put on Pepsi against Coke.

plain: The full order a fund wants to trade, before it is cut into smaller child orders.
desk: The parent's 500k, we'll work it over two days.

plain: Buying a fund that simply copies an index, at very low cost, instead of trying to beat it.
desk: Passive flows are propping up the index.

plain: When a market maker pays a retail broker for the right to fill its customers' orders. Common in US shares; banned in the UK.
desk: Commission-free apps live on payment for order flow.

plain: An order whose price moves automatically to follow a reference, like the best bid or the midpoint.
desk: Rest it on a midpoint peg.

plain: An algo that trades a fixed share, say 10%, of whatever the market trades, so it speeds up when the market is busy and slows when it's quiet.
desk: Put it on a 10% POV.

plain: The share of a fund's profits taken by the manager, usually 15 to 20%, charged only on gains above the high-water mark.
desk: No performance fee this year: we are still below the mark.

plain: The standard small step in an FX price. For most pairs it's the fourth decimal place (0.0001); for yen pairs it's the second (0.01).
desk: EUR/USD is two pips wide.

plain: One portfolio manager and their small team inside a multi-manager platform, running a separate book with its own capital and limits.
desk: They added three new credit pods this quarter.

plain: The one short-term interest rate a central bank sets directly, which all other rates in the economy are built on. Bank Rate in the UK, fed funds in the US, the MPR in Nigeria.
desk: The policy rate is 4%, so two-year gilts can't sit far below it.

plain: How QE works through investors: when the central bank buys bonds, sellers put the money into other assets, pushing their prices up and yields down too.
desk: It's the portfolio balance effect: they bought gilts and we all went into credit.

plain: The person who decides what goes in a portfolio, how big each position is, and when to cut.
desk: Pitch it to the PM at the morning meeting.

plain: Margin worked out from the risk of the whole account, so hedged positions need less. Allows more leverage than fixed rules.
desk: On portfolio margin we can run much more gross.

plain: How investors are already betting in a market: who is long, who is short, and how heavily. Crowded positioning means a sharp move when people exit.
desk: Positioning's stretched: everyone's short yen.

plain: What money you'll get later is worth today.
desk: PV of that cash flow is about seven and a half k.

plain: The market finding the price by pulling buyers and sellers together, rather than anyone deciding it.
desk: The first hour after the news is all price discovery.

plain: The usual rule for who fills first: the best price first, and at the same price, whoever arrived first.
desk: We're at the back of the queue at that level.

plain: News the market already expected, so it's already reflected in the price. Only surprises move it.
desk: The rate cut was fully priced in.

plain: A bank appointed to buy government bonds at auctions and make markets in them, in return for a direct relationship with the central bank or debt office.
desk: The primary dealers took down most of the auction.

plain: Where brand-new shares or bonds are sold for the first time. The issuer gets the money.
desk: Primary's been busy with new bond deals this week.

plain: The part of a bank that serves hedge funds: lending them money and shares, holding their assets and settling their trades.
desk: Our prime broker raised the margin on that position.

plain: A statistical method that finds the few hidden factors explaining most of the movement in many related prices, such as the level, slope and curvature of a yield curve.
desk: Run PCA on the curve and trade the residuals.

plain: Firms that buy whole companies with investors' money and borrowed money, improve them, and sell them a few years later.
desk: It's PE-owned, so they'll look to sell in a few years.

plain: A way of sharing out a trade among everyone waiting at a price in proportion to their size, instead of by who arrived first. Used on some futures markets.
desk: It's pro-rata, so everyone shows more size than they want.

plain: A paid trading evaluation from a retail "prop firm": hit a profit target without breaking loss limits to get a funded account, often simulated, and a share of its profits.
desk: Passed the challenge, but the funded account is still a demo.

plain: Trading a firm's own money for profit, rather than on behalf of clients.
desk: Banks can't do prop any more, it moved to the hedge funds.

plain: Rules that keep financial firms safe, mainly by making them hold enough capital and cash. In the UK, done by the PRA.
desk: The PRA is the prudential regulator, the FCA does conduct.

plain: The right, but not the obligation, to sell something at a set price (the strike) before a set date. It pays out if the price falls below the strike, so it works like insurance.
desk: Nikkei puts as a hedge in case shares sell off.

plain: In the US, a richer category of investor than accredited: at least $5m of investments for a person, or $25m for an institution. Most big hedge funds only take these.
desk: The flagship fund is for qualified purchasers only.

plain: A central bank creating new money to buy government bonds (and sometimes other assets), to push long-term interest rates down when cutting the policy rate isn't enough. Quantitative tightening (QT) reverses it.
desk: QE kept gilt yields pinned for a decade.

plain: The reverse of QE: a central bank shrinking its bond holdings, by letting bonds mature without replacing them (passive) or by selling them (active). It removes reserves from the banking system.
desk: QT's a slow headwind for the long end.

plain: Trading where models decide what to buy or sell, at what price, how much and when, and machines carry most of it out. People design, watch and improve the system rather than making each call.
desk: We moved from discretionary to quant trading three years ago.

plain: The share of an investment's ups and downs explained by something else, usually the market. 0.85 means 85% of its moves are just the market.
desk: R-squared of 0.9: it's an expensive index fund.

plain: The interest rate after taking off inflation: roughly the rate minus inflation. It shows what your money really earns in spending power.
desk: Real rates are still negative in the euro area, so policy isn't tight yet.

plain: Profit or loss that's been locked in by closing a position.
desk: We've realised most of the gain.

plain: Buying and selling to get a portfolio back to its target mix after prices have moved.
desk: Month-end rebalancing flows hit the dollar.

plain: With cash collateral, the interest the lender pays back to the short seller after keeping its fee. A negative rebate means the borrow costs more than the cash earns.
desk: The rebate's minus 20, that's an expensive short.

plain: A lender asking for its lent shares back. The short seller must return them, re-borrowing elsewhere or buying them in the market.
desk: We got a recall ahead of the vote.

plain: The day a company checks its register to see who gets a dividend or other entitlement. Called the qualification date in Nigeria.
desk: Record date's Friday, so it goes ex Thursday.

plain: The share of what's owed that lenders get back after a default, for example 40 cents for every dollar.
desk: Assume 40% recovery on the unsecureds.

plain: Taking money out of a fund by selling your units back to it at the current NAV. Money going in is a subscription.
desk: Q4 redemptions were heavier than we expected.

plain: How far ahead an investor must tell a fund they want to take money out, usually 30 to 90 days.
desk: It's quarterly with 60 days' notice.

plain: George Soros's idea that prices do not just reflect the world but change it, so a trend can feed on itself and push prices far from fair value before it snaps back.
desk: The currency weakness is reflexive: it is causing the outflows it is pricing.

plain: The market's current conditions, its weather: the mix of direction, volatility, interest rates and credit that decides which strategies do well.
desk: This is a different regime: rates matter again.

plain: A way of fitting a straight line through data points to measure how one thing moves with another. For a fund, the slope is its beta and the starting point is its alpha.
desk: Regress the monthly returns on the index and see what's left.

plain: The US rule that you must pay at least 50% of a share purchase with your own money.
desk: Reg T caps you at two times on day one.

plain: An official body that makes and enforces the rules for a market or industry, like the SEC, FCA or CBN.
desk: The regulator wants a report by Friday.

plain: A prime broker reusing a client's collateral for its own lending and funding. In the US it's capped at 140% of what the client owes.
desk: Cap the rehyp in the new prime agreement.

plain: A strategy that buys one security and sells a closely related one, profiting as the price gap between them closes, with little net exposure to the market.
desk: RV books hate low volatility: the spreads are too tight.

plain: Selling a bond and agreeing to buy it back later: a loan secured on the bond. Used to borrow cash, or from the other side, to borrow a bond to short.
desk: That gilt is trading special in repo.

plain: Asking a few dealers for their price, then dealing with whoever's best.
desk: Put it out to five dealers on RFQ.

plain: The most a buyer would pay, or the least a seller would accept, before walking away.
desk: He won't sell below 98: that's his reservation price.

plain: Combining shares into fewer, more expensive ones (for example 10 into 1). Often a warning sign.
desk: A 1-for-10 reverse split, never a good look.

plain: A company offering existing shareholders new shares at a discount, in proportion to what they already own, to raise money.
desk: It's a 1-for-4 rights issue at a 30% discount.

plain: The UK rule, in force since 2019, that separates big banks' everyday retail banking from their riskier investment banking.
desk: That's the ring-fenced bank, it can't trade like that.

plain: How much risk a PM or strategy is allowed to take, set as limits on losses, volatility or exposure.
desk: His risk budget was cut after the drawdown.

plain: The extra return investors expect for putting up with more risk. It's why bumpier assets that pay income have usually paid more over time.
desk: The equity risk premium looks thin at these prices.

plain: A dealer's price for doing the whole amount at once, taking on all the risk. Quick and certain for the client, but wider than working the order.
desk: Show me a risk price on 200 cable.

plain: Where investors trade existing shares and bonds with each other. The issuer gets nothing from these trades.
desk: The new bonds are trading well in the secondary.

plain: Owners like pension funds lending their shares or bonds to others for a fee, against collateral. It's what makes short selling possible.
desk: The lending desk can find you some.

plain: A firm that puts money into a new fund at launch, typically $50m to $200m, in return for a share of the fund firm's revenue or ownership.
desk: They launched with 150 million from a seeder.

plain: Firms that sell financial services (advice, new issues, trading, lending, research) and are paid fees and spreads.
desk: Sell-side research is all bullish on it.

plain: An account owned by one big investor that a manager trades for it, instead of the investor buying into the fund. The investor can see everything and leave at any time.
desk: The pension fund only invests through managed accounts now.

plain: The final step of a trade, when the securities and the cash actually change hands.
desk: Settlement's tomorrow, the cash isn't ours yet.

plain: A trade that doesn't settle on time, usually because the securities weren't delivered.
desk: Our short failed, we're getting bought in.

plain: The risk that you pay your side of a trade and never receive the other side, because the two payments happen at different times.
desk: Use CLS, the Herstatt risk is too big.

plain: A company buying its own shares, leaving fewer shares so each one owns a bigger slice.
desk: They announced a £2bn buyback.

plain: Return above the cash rate divided by volatility: how much return you earned for each unit of risk taken.
desk: A Sharpe above 1 for five years gets you meetings.

plain: The total number of shares currently sold short, often shown as a percentage of the free float.
desk: SI is 25% of float and rising.

plain: Borrowing something, selling it now and buying it back later to return, so you make money if the price falls.
desk: We're short the weakest name in the sector as a hedge.

plain: A rising price forcing short sellers to buy back, whose buying pushes the price higher and forces more of them to buy.
desk: Don't fight it, it's a squeeze, not news.

plain: A private agreement giving one investor different terms from the rest, such as lower fees, more information or faster exits.
desk: Their side letter has a most favoured nation clause.

plain: A separate account inside a fund for assets that are hard to value or sell. Investors are paid out only when those assets are sold.
desk: The private stake went into a side pocket.

plain: A measurable input, such as a ratio, a price pattern or a data feed, that a quant model uses to predict which assets will rise or fall.
desk: The new signal adds 0.2 to the Sharpe.

plain: A signal's returns shrinking over time as more traders find and use it.
desk: That signal's decayed since the paper came out.

plain: A hedge fund where one founder makes the final call on every position.
desk: It's a single-manager shop, so the CIO decides everything.

plain: The gap between the price you expected and the price you actually got.
desk: We slipped 3 ticks on the stop.

plain: Software that checks prices, fees and speed on every venue and splits an order across them for the best overall result.
desk: The SOR sprayed it across six venues in a millisecond.

plain: The Secured Overnight Financing Rate: the main US benchmark for short-term borrowing, based on overnight repo deals in Treasuries. Loans are priced as SOFR plus a spread.
desk: Financing's SOFR plus 50.

plain: Sterling Overnight Index Average: the UK's overnight interest rate benchmark, calculated by the Bank of England from real overnight sterling deposits. It sits just below Bank Rate.
desk: SONIA swaps are pricing another hike by March.

plain: A country's investment fund, often built from oil money or trade surpluses, investing for future generations.
desk: A sovereign wealth fund took a big chunk of the deal.

plain: Investments built around a one-off corporate event rather than a company's normal business, such as spin-offs, rights offerings, lawsuits and restructurings.
desk: It's a special sit: the spin-off's mispriced.

plain: A company turning part of its business into a separate listed company and handing the new shares to its shareholders.
desk: Index funds have to dump the spin-off.

plain: Placing large orders you intend to cancel, to fool others about supply and demand. Illegal.
desk: Surveillance flagged it as possible spoofing.

plain: A crypto token designed to always be worth the same as a normal currency, usually one US dollar.
desk: Clients are settling in dollar stablecoins.

plain: High inflation and a weak economy with rising unemployment at the same time. It's the hardest situation for a central bank, because fighting inflation and protecting jobs need opposite moves.
desk: Oil at these levels is a stagflation shock for Europe.

plain: A measure of how spread out results are around their average: the size of a typical swing. Often called sigma.
desk: Daily P&L standard deviation is about forty thousand.

plain: Market-neutral trading that bets short-term gaps between closely related securities will close, usually across hundreds or thousands of small positions.
desk: The stat arb book holds 3,000 names.

plain: Turning each share into several cheaper ones (for example 2-for-1). The company's value doesn't change.
desk: After the 10-for-1 split it trades around $120.

plain: An order that waits until a trigger price is reached, then becomes a market order. Used to cut losses or to get in on a breakout.
desk: Sell stop at 48, below the lows.

plain: A stop that becomes a limit order when triggered, so it won't sell below its limit but may not sell at all.
desk: Use a stop-limit so it can't fill miles away.

plain: At a platform, the limit on how far a PM's book can fall from its peak before their capital is cut or taken away, typically 5 to 10%.
desk: Down 7.5%, she hit the stop-loss and was out.

plain: Buying a holding company and shorting the listed companies it owns, when the holding company trades below the value of its stakes, so the rest of its business is bought for almost nothing.
desk: The stub's trading at negative value.

plain: When money moves quickly out of one investment style or sector and into another, such as from growth to value in 2022, hurting funds that lean the wrong way.
desk: Brutal rotation into value today; our growth longs got hit.

plain: The Fed's quarterly set of forecasts from each official for growth, unemployment, inflation and the right interest rate. The dot plot is part of it.
desk: The SEP raised the core PCE forecast to 3.4% for this year.

plain: How much people are willing to sell at each price. Drawn as the sellers line, which slopes up.
desk: Supply cuts are pushing oil higher.

plain: The value a trade creates: the gap between what the buyer would pay at most and what the seller would accept at least.
desk: Both sides walked away with some of the surplus.

plain: When a fund stops all withdrawals for a while, usually because it cannot sell assets fast enough or value them fairly.
desk: Three property funds announced suspensions this morning.

plain: The gap between the interest rate on a swap and the yield on a government bond of the same maturity.
desk: 30-year swap spreads went negative after 2008.

plain: Giving a fund exposure through total return swaps instead of owning the shares. More leverage, easier access, less visible.
desk: We run the Asia book synthetic.

plain: Trading where computer rules decide what to buy and sell, such as following trends, with no human calls on individual trades.
desk: The systematic book cut its yen short as soon as the trend turned.

plain: How many business days after the trade date it settles: T+1 is the next business day. US shares are T+1; UK and EU shares T+2 until October 2027.
desk: It's T+1 now, the cash is in tomorrow.

plain: The risk of rare, extreme moves that normal models say are almost impossible.
desk: Buy some puts against the tail risk.

plain: The side of a trade that arrived and traded against an order already waiting. Takers pay the spread for getting done straight away.
desk: We were takers all morning, it cost us.

plain: A rule of thumb for the policy rate: the neutral real rate, plus inflation, plus half of inflation's gap from target, plus half the output gap. A yardstick, not something central banks follow exactly.
desk: On a Taylor Rule basis they're still a point too low.

plain: An offer to buy shares straight from shareholders at a set price, usually above the market, from the company itself or a buyer.
desk: The tender's oversubscribed, we'll only get half filled.

plain: The extra interest lenders want for lending for longer, beyond what they expect short-term rates to average, because more can go wrong over a long time.
desk: The long end's selling off on term premium, not on the Fed.

plain: The price a share should settle at after a rights issue: a blend of the old price and the cheap new shares.
desk: TERP is 94, so each right's worth 24.

plain: How much an option loses in value each day just from time passing, all else equal. It is the cost of holding gamma.
desk: Gamma's good but theta's eating us on quiet days.

plain: Every individual quote and trade, timestamped: the most detailed price history there is.
desk: You'll need tick data to test anything intraday.

plain: A manager who trained at Julian Robertson's Tiger Management and went on to start their own fund, such as Viking Global, Tiger Global or Coatue.
desk: She is a Tiger grandcub: trained at Viking.

plain: How long an order stays live: day, good-till-cancelled, immediate-or-cancel, or fill-or-kill.
desk: What's the time in force on that?

plain: The idea that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future, because it can earn interest, because of inflation, and because a future payment might not arrive.
desk: It's all time value of money: discount the cash flows and compare.

plain: An algo that trades equal amounts at regular times through a window, whatever the volume.
desk: No volume data in FX, so just TWAP it over the hour.

plain: The risk that the price moves away from you while a big order is still being worked. The slower you trade, the bigger it gets.
desk: Too much timing risk to sit on it all day.

plain: A contract that pays you the gains and losses of an asset without you owning it, in return for a financing fee. Lets funds take leveraged positions quietly.
desk: Archegos held it all through total return swaps.

plain: The history of a manager's real returns over time, which investors check before trusting them with money.
desk: They need three years of track record before the consultants will look.

plain: A mortgage whose rate moves automatically with the central bank's rate, for example Bank Rate plus 1%.
desk: Trackers reprice from next month; fixes only when they roll off.

plain: Scoring every order after it's done against benchmarks like the decision price and VWAP, to see which algos and brokers work best.
desk: Pull the TCA on that broker.

plain: The routes by which a change in the central bank's rate reaches the economy: borrowing costs, asset prices, the exchange rate, bank lending and expectations.
desk: Transmission is slower this cycle because so many people fixed.

plain: The classic hedge fund fee: 2% of assets a year plus 20% of the profits. The average today is nearer 1.4% and 17%.
desk: Nobody gets 2 and 20 any more except the very best.

plain: Gold held as a promise from a bank to deliver it, like a deposit. Cheaper than allocated (specific bars in your name), but you're a creditor if the bank fails.
desk: Unallocated is fine for trading, allocated for keeping.

plain: The thing a derivative's price comes from. For a gold future, the underlying is gold.
desk: Where's the underlying trading?

plain: An investment bank that runs a new issue of shares or bonds, finds the buyers and helps set the price.
desk: We're one of three underwriters on the deal.

plain: A company's share price before any takeover bid was announced or rumoured. Traders use it to estimate where the shares would fall if the deal broke.
desk: Undisturbed was 35, so the downside is 12.

plain: Profit or loss on positions you still hold, at today's prices. A paper loss is still a loss.
desk: It's unrealised, but it's real.

plain: A US tax that can hit normally tax-free investors, like endowments, on income from a partnership that borrows money. Investing through an offshore company blocks it.
desk: The endowment comes in through the offshore feeder for UBTI reasons.

plain: The share of all lendable stock that's already out on loan. Above about 90%, new shorts struggle to borrow.
desk: Utilisation's at 95%, the borrow's about to get expensive.

plain: The tendency of cheap shares (low price compared with earnings or book value) to beat expensive ones over long periods, though it can lag for years.
desk: Value had a brutal 2020 and a great 2022.

plain: A specific, evidence-backed view that differs from the consensus, with a reason the market will come round to it.
desk: What's your variant perception here?

plain: Gains and losses on a cleared position paid in cash every day (or during the day), so losses can't build up unseen.
desk: VM call is big today, check the cash.

plain: An arrow, or just a list of numbers like [2, 1].
desk: Send me the positions vector.

plain: How much a price jumps around. Usually measured as the standard deviation of returns.
desk: Vol's picked up since the data.

plain: The US rule, part of the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act, that bans big banks from proprietary trading.
desk: Post-Volcker, the bank only makes markets.

plain: The average price of every trade in a period, with bigger trades counting more. Also an algo that trades in line with the usual volume pattern to match it.
desk: We bought them a cent under VWAP.

plain: A large market order taking all the shares at the best price, then the next price, and so on, getting a worse average each step.
desk: That size will walk the book, so work it.

plain: When people spend more because their homes or investments have gone up in value, or less because they've fallen.
desk: Equities down 15% will take some heat out of spending through the wealth effect.

plain: A trade that looks logical but has ruined many who tried it, usually because it takes far longer to work than funds can wait. The classic one is shorting Japanese government bonds.
desk: Shorting JGBs was the widowmaker for 20 years.

plain: The approach made famous by Yale's endowment of putting a large share of a long-term portfolio into alternatives such as hedge funds, private equity and property.
desk: The pension fund moved towards the Yale Model and doubled its hedge fund allocation.

plain: A line showing the interest rate on government bonds of different lengths, from months to decades. Usually long rates are higher; when short rates are higher, the curve is inverted.
desk: The curve's inverted: markets expect cuts.

plain: A central bank naming a target for a longer-term bond yield and buying as many bonds as needed to hold it there. The Bank of Japan capped its 10-year yield near 0% from 2016 to 2024.
desk: YCC kept JGBs pinned while the yen fell.

plain: The single interest rate that makes a bond's discounted payments add up to its price: the return you earn if you buy now, hold to the end and every payment arrives. The standard way bonds are quoted.
desk: Tens are yielding 5.3 to maturity.

plain: How many standard deviations a value sits above or below its average. Stat arb often enters trades when a spread's z-score passes plus or minus 2.
desk: The spread's at a z of 2.3; put it on.

plain: A bond that pays no coupons, only its face value at maturity. It's bought for less than face value, and the gap is the interest.
desk: Strip the coupons and you've got a 30-year zero.
